title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals have deployed generative AI and voice-cloning technology to impersonate real people, including a South Florida immigration attorney, in order to defraud victims. The impersonation happens on social media and over the phone, where scammers use cloned voices and fabricated credentials to pose as legal professionals offering immigration services. Victims lost money by sending funds to accounts they believed belonged to legitimate attorneys.

This is a failure of AI systems to remain restricted to their intended uses. Voice synthesis and video generation tools built for legitimate purposes were repurposed to commit fraud at scale. The deployment occurred entirely outside the systems' original context, in criminal schemes rather than authorized applications. Catching this would have required either technical controls to prevent voice and identity cloning, or monitoring of how these tools were actually being used in the wild.

It is not established whether the AI systems were sold or licensed to the criminals, whether they were stolen or accessed without authorization, or what specific platforms or tools were used.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit sophisticated scams across Georgia and South Florida. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. Notable cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to target immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. In Florida alone, there were 350 AI-related complaints totaling $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints with $10.4 million in losses. Authorities note these figures likely undercount the actual problem since many victims never report being scammed.

Scammers are using generative AI to make traditional fraud schemes far more convincing by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching personal relationships. Common schemes include grandparent scams using voice-cloning technology and romance scams. Financial institutions warn customers that AI is making impersonation attempts increasingly difficult to detect. To protect themselves, consumers should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests by calling known numbers, never send money based on phone calls alone, and report suspected scams to law enforcement and the FBI.
